questions.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
questions.title: var, let, and const
questions.direct_answer: var creates a function-scoped binding and allows redeclaration, while let and const create block-scoped bindings. let permits reassignment; const does not. const protects the binding, not the object stored behind it, so a const array or object may still be mutated.

interviewer_intent.testing: Scope, reassignment, redeclaration, and temporal dead zone semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a const object as deeply immutable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguishing declaration hoisting from safe access before initialization.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped.
let can be reassigned; const must be initialized and cannot be reassigned.
var can be redeclared in the same scope; let and const cannot.
const freezes the binding, not the contents of an object.
let and const cannot be read before initialization because of the temporal dead zone.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `var` is function-scoped, so a declaration inside an `if` block still belongs to the surrounding function. It may be redeclared and its binding is initialized to `undefined` before execution reaches the declaration.

- `let` and `const` are block-scoped. `let` is for a binding that must point to a different value later, while `const` must receive a value at declaration and cannot be reassigned. Both exist in a temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.

- `const` does not make an object immutable. For example, `const user = { name: "Ada" }` prevents `user = otherUser`, but `user.name = "Grace"` is allowed because the binding still points to the same object.

- I normally begin with `const` because a stable binding makes changes easier to track, and move to `let` only when reassignment is part of the algorithm. I avoid `var` in new code because its function scope and redeclaration rules make accidental state changes harder to see.

sections.title: A variable declaration creates a binding
sections.content: A JavaScript variable is a named binding to a value. Scope decides where the name can be used; reassignment decides whether that binding may later point elsewhere. These rules are separate from whether the value itself—such as an object—can change.

sections.title: Initialization and the temporal dead zone
sections.content:
Before a scope begins executing, JavaScript creates bindings for its declarations. A `var` binding is initialized with `undefined`, which is why reading it early produces `undefined`. A `let` or `const` binding is created but remains uninitialized until evaluation reaches its declaration. Reading it during that interval throws a `ReferenceError`; that interval is the temporal dead zone.

At global script level, top-level `var` also becomes a property of `globalThis` in browsers, while top-level `let` and `const` do not. In an ES module, top-level declarations stay in module scope.

sections.title: Declaration rules
sections.content:
| Declaration | Scope | Reassign | Redeclare in same scope | Read before declaration |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `var` | Function or global | Yes | Yes | `undefined` |
| `let` | Block | Yes | No | `ReferenceError` |
| `const` | Block | No | No | `ReferenceError` |

questions.question: What is the difference between primitive values and objects in JavaScript?
questions.title: Primitive values and objects
questions.direct_answer: JavaScript primitives are immutable values: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null. Objects are mutable collections of properties. Assignment copies a primitive value, but for an object it copies the reference value, so two variables may refer to the same object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Value semantics, reference sharing, identity, and mutation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying that JavaScript passes objects by reference rather than passing a reference value by value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explaining that spread syntax makes a shallow copy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: There are seven primitive types; everything else is an object.
Primitive values are immutable and assignment copies the value.
Object assignment copies a reference value, not the object's properties.
Objects compare by identity, even when their contents look equal.
Spread and Object.assign create shallow, not deep, copies.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- A primitive is a single immutable value. JavaScript has `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `null`; changing a string actually creates a new string rather than editing the old one.

- Objects—including arrays and functions—can hold properties and can be mutated. Assignment still works by value in JavaScript, but the value being copied for an object is a reference to that object. That is why two variables can observe the same mutation.

- For example, after `const b = a`, changing `b.name` also appears through `a` when both names refer to the same object. In contrast, copying a number and incrementing the copy does not change the original number.

- Equality follows the same distinction: two separate object literals are not strictly equal, even if their properties match, while equal primitive values normally compare equal. When isolation is needed, I create a copy, but I remember that object spread copies only the first level; nested objects remain shared unless they are copied too.

sections.title: Values are copied; some values point to objects
sections.content: JavaScript does not copy an entire object during ordinary assignment. It copies the reference value. This model explains shared mutation without inventing a separate pass-by-reference rule for function arguments.

sections.title: Identity, mutation, and shallow copying
sections.content:
An object has identity independent of its properties. `{ score: 1 } === { score: 1 }` is false because the expressions create two different objects. If both variables hold the same reference value, strict equality is true and mutations are visible through either name.

A spread expression such as `{ ...user }` creates a new outer object and copies enumerable own properties into it. A nested address object is still the same nested object in both copies. `structuredClone` can deeply copy many built-in data types, but it cannot clone functions and is not a universal replacement for choosing an intentional data model.

sections.title: What assignment copies
sections.content:
| Value | Assignment copies | Can the value itself mutate? | Equality usually checks |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Primitive | The primitive value | No | Value |
| Object | A reference value | Yes | Identity |

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
questions.title: null and undefined
questions.direct_answer: undefined usually means that JavaScript or the program has not supplied a value, while null is an explicit value commonly used to represent an intentional absence. They are different primitive values: null == undefined is true because of one special loose-equality rule, but null === undefined is false.

interviewer_intent.testing: Missing-value semantics and safe equality checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using truthiness when zero, false, or an empty string are valid values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explaining the historical typeof null result and nullish coalescing.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: undefined commonly represents a value that was not provided.
null commonly represents an absence chosen by the program or API.
null and undefined are distinct primitive values.
Use value == null only when intentionally matching both nullish values.
The expression typeof null returns "object" because of a historical language bug.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `undefined` is the default missing value in many language operations. A declared variable without an initializer, a missing object property, and a function with no return statement all produce `undefined`.

- `null` is normally assigned deliberately to mean “there is no object or value here.” The exact business meaning should be part of the API contract; a database result might use `null` for a known empty field and omit another field entirely.

- They are separate primitives, so `null === undefined` is false. A special loose-equality rule makes `null == undefined` true, which can be useful only when a check is intentionally meant to accept either nullish value.

- For example, `name ?? "Guest"` supplies a default only for `null` or `undefined`, while `name || "Guest"` also replaces valid falsy values such as an empty string. I use an explicit check when those states have different meanings, and I do not rely on `typeof null` because its historical result is `"object"`.

sections.title: Absence needs a contract
sections.content: The useful difference is not merely syntax: it is who chose the missing state and what callers should do with it. Consistent APIs distinguish “not supplied,” “looked up and absent,” and valid falsy data.

sections.title: Defaulting without losing valid data
sections.content:
Truthiness merges several unrelated values: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, an empty string, `NaN`, `null`, and `undefined` are all falsy. A default built with `||` can therefore erase real data. The nullish coalescing operator `??` narrows the fallback to `null` and `undefined`. Optional chaining returns `undefined` when its left side is nullish, which often pairs naturally with `??`.

JSON introduces another boundary: an object property whose value is `undefined` is omitted by `JSON.stringify`, while a property containing `null` is preserved. That difference can change a patch request from “leave this field unchanged” to “clear this field.”

sections.title: Common sources and behaviour
sections.content:
| Value | Common meaning | `typeof` | Kept in JSON object? |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `undefined` | Not supplied or not produced | `"undefined"` | No |
| `null` | Intentionally empty | `"object"` | Yes |

sections.title: Choose a nullish check deliberately
sections.content:
```javascript
const settings = { retries: 0, label: "", owner: null };

console.log(settings.retries ?? 3); // 0
console.log(settings.retries || 3); // 3: often an accidental fallback
console.log(settings.owner == null); // true for null or undefined
console.log(settings.label === undefined); // false
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: null })); // {"b":null}
```
